readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Evacuation Center Act of 2022 requires the Bangsamoro Government to build a standard evacuation center in every municipality and city in the region.

The Ministry of Public Works prepares the standard design and the construction, working from the Philippine building code. Each center must stand in a safe and accessible place in the town and accommodate at least 100 to 200 internally displaced people. It must have proper ventilation, a kitchen, water, plumbing and sanitation, and facilities for women — breastfeeding mothers are named — for the elderly and for people with special needs.

Management sits with the Ministry of Social Services and Development, delivered on the ground by the Municipal or City Social Welfare and Development Officer, who gets a designated office inside the center that doubles as their municipal office. The local government complements MSSD’s manpower through the municipal disaster risk reduction officer.

The centers are also meant to work between disasters: the objectives include giving each local government a designated place for prepositioning, stocking, repacking and piling relief goods, so supplies are staged before an emergency rather than moved during one.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is a single line about safety and general welfare in crisis and disaster situations. The explanatory note is more specific: the Philippines is disaster-prone and the Bangsamoro carries typhoons, floods, landslides, earthquakes and drought, along with fires and displacement caused by armed groups. It opens with a hadith on relieving a believer of the hardships of this world.

The practical problem it addresses is one every disaster in this region exposes. In the absence of purpose-built centers, displaced families are housed in schools and covered courts — which closes the schools, provides no sanitation for the numbers involved, and gives no privacy at all.
whoIsAffected: Displaced families across the region, who currently shelter in schools and covered courts.
Women and breastfeeding mothers, the elderly and people with special needs, named for specific facilities.
Every municipality and city in BARMM, each of which would host a center.
Municipal and City Social Welfare and Development Officers, who would manage the centers and be based in them.
Schools, which would stop being the default shelter.
Basilan and Marawi City, where social welfare services are already devolved and which the Act only encourages rather than binds.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW), for the standard design and construction
Ministry of Social Services and Development (MSSD), which supervises the centers
Municipal and City Social Welfare and Development Officers, who manage them
Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officers, who complement MSSD manpower

funding.detail: No figure. Construction, operation and maintenance are to be included in the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region. A purpose-built center in each of the region’s municipalities and cities is a large capital program, and the bill states neither a total nor a per-unit cost.

whatChanges: Every municipality and city in the region is to have a standard evacuation center.
A standard design exists, drawn by MPW against the national building code.
Centers must hold at least 100 to 200 people and carry kitchen, water, sanitation and facilities for women, the elderly and people with special needs.
MSSD supervises and the municipal or city social welfare officer manages, from an office inside the center.
Local governments gain a designated place to preposition and repack relief goods.
readings.insight:
The capacity figure is the thing to look at hardest. A center built for 100 to 200 people is the right size for a barangay-scale flood and nowhere near the right size for what this region actually experiences. The 2017 Marawi siege displaced roughly 200,000 people; a single bad flood season in the Maguindanao lowlands displaces tens of thousands. One center per municipality at 200 heads is a floor worth having and should not be mistaken for a plan that meets the region’s largest events.

Section 8 contains an odd carve-out. The Act covers all municipalities and cities in the region, but where social welfare has already been devolved to the local government — the bill names Basilan province and Marawi City — those LGUs are merely "encouraged" to implement it. Marawi is the site of the largest displacement in the region’s recent history, and it is the one place the Act does not bind.

The office-inside-the-center provision is quietly clever and easy to miss. Putting the social welfare officer’s permanent municipal office in the evacuation center means the building is occupied, staffed and maintained between emergencies rather than standing empty and deteriorating, which is how most single-purpose emergency structures fail.

On its progress: filed September 2022, First Reading January 2023, and then referred to the Committee on Local Government in July 2025 — two and a half years between reading and referral.

readings.whatItDoes:
This breaks the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform into three bodies and writes a charter for each: the Bangsamoro Ministry of Agriculture, the Bangsamoro Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, and the Bangsamoro Agrarian Reform Office. It does this by amending the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13.

The bill is built as five books. Book I sets the policy and performs the separation itself in a single section. Books II, III and IV are full organizational charters — mandate, powers and functions, organizational structure, the offices of the minister and deputy minister, a director general, bureaus and divisions, provincial offices, city and municipal offices, and the qualifications required of every one of those posts. Book V holds the miscellaneous provisions.

Each of the three gets its own field structure down to the municipality, its own authority over those field offices, its own arrangements for coordinating with attached agencies and with agriculture-related national agencies that were never devolved, and its own handling of nationally funded and foreign-assisted programs and of agricultural technicians deployed to local governments.

Book V settles the consequences. Affected officials and employees are compensated under existing law. Each of the three agencies gets a separate budget item in the annual appropriations act. The Office of the Chief Minister issues the implementing rules. A mandatory review falls due after 10 years, and Parliament is given a standing oversight function over the whole thing.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues from the size of the sector. It cites the 2021 Gross Regional Domestic Product: BARMM is predominantly services-based at 38.9%, but agriculture, forestry and fishing follow immediately at 36.4%, ahead of industry at 24.7% — and the sector was accelerating, from 2.7% growth between 2019 and 2020 to 8.3% in the following period. It runs the constitutional argument alongside: Article XII on industrialisation founded on sound agricultural development and agrarian reform, the fisheries provision on small-scale utilization with priority to subsistence fisherfolk, and Article II Section 21 on comprehensive rural development.

The implicit case is that one ministry carrying agriculture, fisheries and agrarian reform together cannot give any of the three the attention a sector that size requires.
whoIsAffected: Farmers, fisherfolk and agrarian reform beneficiaries across the region, in a sector that is over a third of regional output.
Employees and officials of the existing MAFAR, who would be distributed across three bodies and are promised compensation under existing rules.
Local government units, which receive deployed agricultural technicians and host the new city and municipal offices.
Agrarian reform beneficiaries specifically, whose function moves to an Office rather than to a Ministry.
National agencies with agriculture-related mandates that were never devolved, with which each new body must coordinate separately.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Ministry of Agriculture (B-MOA), with a Minister, Deputy Minister, Director General, bureaus and divisions, and provincial, city and municipal offices
Bangsamoro Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (B-MFAR), on the same pattern
Bangsamoro Agrarian Reform Office (BARO), headed by a Regional Director with an Assistant Regional Director, services, and city and municipal offices
Office of the Chief Minister, which issues the implementing rules
The Bangsamoro Parliament, given a standing oversight function and a mandatory review at 10 years

funding.detail: No figure, and no transitional cost estimate. Book V says only that funding for the three agencies shall be included in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro in a separate budget item for each. Standing up two ministries and an office where one ministry stood — with provincial, city and municipal structures for each — carries a cost the bill never attempts to state.

whatChanges: MAFAR ceases to exist as a single ministry and becomes three bodies.
Agriculture and fisheries each acquire a ministry with its own minister, deputy minister and director general.
Agrarian reform becomes an Office headed by a Regional Director rather than a Ministry.
Each body gains its own provincial, city and municipal field structure.
Book I, Title I of the Bangsamoro Administrative Code is amended to match.
Each of the three gets a separate line in the annual appropriations act.
A mandatory review falls due 10 years after implementation begins.
readings.insight:
The asymmetry is the story. Two of the three come out of this as ministries, with a Minister, a Deputy Minister and a Director General; the third — agrarian reform — comes out as an Office headed by a Regional Director. A bill presented as separating three functions so each can be attended to properly in fact elevates two of them and leaves the third at a lower rank than the ministry it left. In a region where land tenure and ancestral domain are among the most contested questions there are, that is not a filing detail.

The title carries a naming wobble worth knowing about before anyone cites it. The title of the bill names the second body the Bangsamoro Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources; the operative section that performs the split calls it the "Bangsamoro-Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Office" — a ministry and an office in the same breath.

And the money is missing in the place it matters most. This is a reorganization bill: its entire cost is transitional — new offices, new posts, new field structures in every province and municipality, and compensation for displaced staff. The bill mentions the compensation and then says the funding goes in the appropriations act in three separate line items. What the separation costs to carry out is the one number a reader would want and the bill does not have it.

On its progress: filed in October 2022, First Reading in January 2023, and then nothing on the index until November 2025, when it reached Second Reading and was referred to the Committees on Amendments, Revision and Codification of Laws and on Finance. Nearly 3 years between readings is on the long side even for this Parliament.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Commission on Population Management and Development, attached to the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, to recommend, plan, coordinate, implement and monitor population and development policy in the region.

The bill models it explicitly on the national Commission on Population and Development, which sits under the National Economic and Development Authority, and says the Bangsamoro body shall have the same set-up so the mechanism runs cleanly from national to local level. It sets guiding principles — human beings at the center of sustainable development, population goals as an integral part of the region’s cultural, economic and social development, and a right to an adequate standard of living including food, clothing, housing, education, water and sanitation.

Beneath that it provides for duties and functions, an Executive Director with stated powers, programs under a Population Management and Development Office, and the acceptance of donations and grants.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy anchors it in the Philippines’ commitments as a signatory to the UN International Conference on Population and Development, and in Republic Act 10354, the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act of 2012 — recognizing the right to decide freely and responsibly on the number and spacing of children within responsible parenthood and informed choice, and to access reproductive health information and services.

The developmental case is stated alongside: better health outcomes, and meeting the socio-demographic and economic challenges of a region with among the highest fertility and youngest population profiles in the country.
whoIsAffected: Families across the region, as the intended subject of population and development programming.
The Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, which would host the Commission.
Health and social services ministries, whose programs would be coordinated through it.
Local government units, through the national-to-local mechanism the bill wants replicated.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission on Population Management and Development, attached to the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
A Population Management and Development Office running the programs
An Executive Director with powers, duties and responsibilities set out in the Act

funding.detail: The bill’s title says it appropriates funds. The filed text has no appropriations section — it runs from programs to donations and grants to rules and regulations, repeal, suppletory clause, separability and effectivity. What it does provide for is the acceptance of donations and grants, which is not the same thing as an appropriation.

whatChanges: A regional commission on population and development exists, attached to BPDA.
Population policy is coordinated regionally rather than run out of national programs alone.
A Population Management and Development Office runs the programs.
The Commission may accept donations and grants.
readings.insight:
The name does not settle. Section 1 calls the statute the "Bangsamoro Commission on Population and Development Act of 2022"; Section 3 creates the "Bangsamoro Commission on Population Management and Development". The title on Parliament’s index uses the longer form. "Management" is not a neutral extra word in this context, and a body whose own charter names it two ways is a problem before it starts.

The title also promises an appropriation the text does not make. "Appropriating Funds Therefore" is in the title on the index; there is no appropriations section in the filed copy.

The substance is more delicate than the drafting. This is a Government of the Day bill grounding a population commission in the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act — a national law that was among the most contested in recent Philippine history, and one whose reception in a Muslim-majority region involves questions of religious teaching the bill does not engage with at all. The framing chosen is telling: population *management and development*, guiding principles about standard of living and human potential, and an institutional home in the planning authority rather than in health. Whether that framing survives committee is the interesting question, and the bill was referred to the Committees on Finance and on Rules in September 2024 — nearly 2 years after First Reading.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 121, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Commission for Senior Citizens to carry out senior citizen law and policy inside the region.

The Commission is to ensure the full implementation of laws, policies and programs on senior citizens, review them, and recommend action to the Bangsamoro Government. Its stated objectives run from recognizing the place of older people in society and supporting their full participation, to encouraging families and communities to care for them, to providing a comprehensive health care and rehabilitation system for disabled senior citizens, and to bringing the private sector in as a partner.

Beneath the objectives the bill provides for a site of office, an organizational structure, a Regional Director with stated powers, office personnel, and core programs. It is drawn to be consistent with the principles and objectives of the national Commission of Senior Citizens, and it defines a senior citizen by reference to Republic Act 9994 — any resident citizen at least 60 years old.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section builds from the Constitution — adequate social services, a rising standard of living, social justice, and the family’s duty to care for elderly members with the State assisting through programs and social security — and then to Section 23, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which requires the Bangsamoro Government to support the welfare of senior citizens and uphold the benefits and privileges they already enjoy.

The practical gap is enforcement. Senior citizen benefits are national law; whether an older person in a municipality in Basilan or Lanao del Sur actually receives them depends on someone regionally being responsible for seeing that they do, and no such office exists.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region aged 60 and over.
Disabled senior citizens specifically, for whom a comprehensive health care and rehabilitation system is an objective.
Families and communities, whom the bill sets out to encourage in caring for older members.
Local government units, where community-based health and rehabilitation programs are to be established in every political unit.
The private sector, named as a partner to be actively sought.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for Senior Citizens, headed by a Regional Director
The Commission’s office personnel and core programs

funding.detail: No figure. The Bangsamoro Government is to appropriate a regular budget for the office and its activities, with the proviso that all national programs under the Act are funded by the national government. That proviso is the load-bearing part: most senior citizen benefits are national entitlements, so the bill funds the regional office and leaves the benefits themselves on the national ledger.

whatChanges: The region gains a commission responsible for senior citizen law and policy.
A Regional Director and office structure exist to review implementation and recommend action.
Community-based health and rehabilitation programs are to be established in every political unit.
The Commission is aligned with the national Commission of Senior Citizens rather than duplicating it.
readings.insight:
The proviso in the appropriations section does most of the work and repays reading twice. The Bangsamoro Government funds the office; the national government funds the national programs the office oversees. That is the right division on paper — the benefits are national entitlements — and it also means the Commission’s power is entirely one of oversight and recommendation. It can find that a municipality is not delivering the 20% discount or the social pension; it cannot fund either.

The drafting is untidy in a way a committee should tidy. The bill runs Section 4, then Section 5 headed "Objectives and Functions", and then doubles back to Sections 4.1 and 4.2 — which is where the Commission’s actual functions are set out. The functions of the body being created sit under a numbering that suggests they belong to the preceding section.

One small thing that dates the text: Section 4.2 has the Commission recommending actions and policies to the "Bangsamoro Transition Authority and Bangsamoro Government". The BTA was the interim body; the region held its first parliamentary election in 2025. A bill filed in November 2022 could not have known that, but the clause reads oddly now.

The measure was enhanced in March 2023 before First Reading, and referred to the Committees on Social Services and Development and on Finance in July 2025.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 124, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This builds a register of skilled workers in the Bangsamoro, from the barangay upwards.

Every barangay in BARMM is responsible for registering the skilled workers in its area, onsite or online, and for setting its own plans and guidelines for gathering the information. The bill defines skilled workers as those with specialised skills, training and knowledge, and — for its own purposes — narrows that to work usually involving physical strength: it names carpenters, welders, plumbers, artisans, handweavers and drivers.

The register records name, ethnic affiliation, address, contact details, skills, trainings attended, certifications, employment experience, and any other necessary detail. No fee of any kind may be charged for registering.

The data then travels up a chain the bill sets out step by step: barangays submit to the municipal or city Public Employment Service Office, which consolidates and submits to the provincial PESO, which consolidates and submits to the Bureau of Employment, Promotions and Welfare of the regional labour ministry. Highly urbanised and independent cities consolidate separately. The Bureau is named the sole repository of data on all registered workers in BARMM.

The rest is data governance: a period of compliance, sharing of data for employment and data matching, a prohibition on unlawful processing, rules on access to the registry, and annual updating.
readings.whyProposed: The gap is that nobody knows what skills the region has. Employment services can only match people to work if there is a list, and the labour ministry’s market information system has no bottom rung. Building the register at barangay level is the bill’s answer: the barangay is the only unit that actually knows who in the community welds, drives or weaves.
whoIsAffected: Skilled workers across the region — the bill names carpenters, welders, plumbers, artisans, handweavers and drivers — who register free of charge.
Every barangay in BARMM, which carries the registration duty and must write its own guidelines for it.
Public Employment Service Offices at municipal, city and provincial level, which consolidate and pass the data up.
The Ministry of Labor and Employment’s Bureau of Employment, Promotions and Welfare, named sole repository.
Employers looking to hire locally, who gain a searchable pool.
implementedBy: Barangays, which register the workers
Municipal, city and provincial Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs), which consolidate
Bureau of Employment, Promotions, and Welfare, MOLE-BARMM, as sole repository

funding.detail: The filed bill has no appropriations section. It runs from annual updating straight to the separability clause and effectivity. Every barangay in the region is given a data collection duty, and the cost of discharging it is not addressed.

whatChanges: Every barangay must register the skilled workers in its area.
Registration is free — the bill prohibits charging any fee.
Data flows barangay → municipal or city PESO → provincial PESO → the regional labour bureau.
The Bureau of Employment, Promotions and Welfare becomes the sole repository for the region.
The registry is updated annually and access to it is regulated.
Unlawful processing of the collected data is prohibited.
readings.insight:
The data protection provisions are the most interesting thing here, and they are better than the bill is often given credit for: a prohibition on unlawful processing, rules on who may access the registry, and a defined purpose of employment matching. That matters because of one field in Section 4 — ethnic affiliation. Collecting ethnicity alongside name, address and contact details, in a region with this history, is a decision with consequences well beyond employment matching, and the bill collects it without saying why it is needed or restricting what it may be used for. A committee should ask.

The definition is the second thing. The bill defines skilled workers broadly and then, "for purposes of this act", narrows them to work usually involving physical strength. That leaves out the region’s teachers, nurses, technicians and IT workers — plausibly deliberate, since the target is the informal trades, but it means the registry will not be what its name suggests to anyone reading the title.

The third is the absence of money. Every barangay in BARMM is directed to design and run a data collection exercise, and no appropriation accompanies the duty. Barangays are the least resourced unit of government in the country, and an unfunded region-wide data mandate discharged 2,590 different ways will produce a register of uneven quality at best.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the cabinet bill that became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 48. It proposes a new municipality, Ligawasan, built from seven barangays of Pikit, North Cotabato — Bagoinged, Barungis, Bulol, Buliok, Gli-Gli, Kabasalan, and Rajamuda — all of which voted in the 2019 plebiscite to join the Bangsamoro and now sit in the region's Special Geographic Areas.

The bill separates those barangays from Pikit and constitutes them as a distinct municipality, with its seat of government at Barangay Bagoinged and a boundary following the existing barangay lines. Annexed tables give the detail: about 112 square kilometers, roughly 29,800 residents, and combined annual income of about ₱31.6 million as of 2020.

The municipality would come into existence only after a plebiscite held within 60 days of approval, conducted by the Commission on Elections through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, and only if a majority of votes cast approve. Until an election, the first mayor, vice-mayor, and council would be appointed.

Because a new municipality gets no share of national revenue immediately, the bill commits the Bangsamoro Government to provide financial assistance of not less than ₱2,500,000 every month for the new local government's administration and operation, until its revenue share is allocated.
readings.whyProposed: The seven barangays voted in 2019 to move from North Cotabato into the Bangsamoro but remained administratively attached to Pikit, a municipality outside the region. The bill invokes the Bangsamoro Government's power to create and alter municipalities and gives those barangays a local government inside the region they voted to join.
whoIsAffected: Roughly 29,800 residents of the seven barangays, across about 112 square kilometers.
The Municipality of Pikit, North Cotabato, which would lose the seven barangays.
Elected officials of Pikit residing in those barangays, whose positions the bill addresses.
The Bangsamoro Government, which would carry at least ₱2.5 million a month until national revenue sharing begins.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which would conduct and supervise the plebiscite
The Bangsamoro Government, which would appropriate the monthly assistance
Appointed first municipal officials, pending an election

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 per month from the Bangsamoro Government until the new municipality is allocated its share of national revenue. Plebiscite expenses are to be taken from available COMELEC funds under its current appropriation.

whatChanges: Seven barangays leave Pikit and form a municipality, subject to the plebiscite.
A new local government is stood up at Bagoinged, appointed at first.
The Bangsamoro Government takes on a monthly financial commitment with a stated floor.
The region's Special Geographic Areas gain a municipality of their own.
readings.insight: This bill is worth comparing with the act it became. The ₱2.5 million monthly floor written here does not survive into Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 48, which promises monthly assistance without naming an amount. If you want to know what a new municipality in the Special Geographic Areas is actually guaranteed, the answer is in the act, not in this bill — and it is less specific than what was filed.
