Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 48, enacted text
Parliament Bill No. 142, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets up a Madaris Education Fund Assistance — a fund for private Islamic schools covering infrastructure, scholarships, teacher development and accreditation.

The assistance is awarded against criteria the bill lists: continuous teacher training, infrastructure facilities, scholarship grants, the socio-economic needs of students with priority to the poorest, the school’s overall performance, and the academic qualifications and financial needs of both students and teachers.

What the fund pays for is set out as 10 items: a nutrition and feeding program for young children; classroom facilities down to desks, tables and chalkboards; textbook assistance at a ratio of one book per student per subject; an in-service training fund for teachers; scholarship grants to children of teachers; scholarship grants to qualified students; funding for training and seminars for Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education teachers; an increase in ALIVE teachers’ salaries; funding for madaris registration and accreditation; and madrasah infrastructure development.

MBHTE issues the rules, in coordination with other agencies.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section recognizes the complementary role of private educational institutions and the contribution madaris make to educating the region’s children, and commits to a fund system for their infrastructure, scholarships, teacher development and accreditation, with subsidies aimed particularly at the underprivileged. It also commits the government to encouraging non-formal, informal and indigenous learning systems.

The underlying problem is the same one Bills 167 and 168 address: madaris teach a large share of Bangsamoro children, sit outside the public funding system, and have no standing route to regional money.
whoIsAffected: Madaris across the region, for infrastructure, textbooks, classroom furniture and accreditation costs.
ALIVE teachers — Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education — who would receive training funds and a salary increase.
Teachers in madaris generally, through an in-service training fund and scholarships for their children.
Students, through scholarships, textbooks at one book per subject, and a feeding program for the young ones.
MBHTE’s Bureau of Madaris, which would administer the fund out of its own current appropriation.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education (MBHTE), which issues the rules
MBHTE Bureau of Madaris, against whose current appropriations the fund is charged

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 for initial implementation, provided in the Bangsamoro Appropriation Act and charged under the current appropriations of the MBHTE Bureau of Madaris. It is one of the few bills in this group to carry a figure at all — and it is a small one against a list of 10 funded items that includes region-wide infrastructure development, one textbook per student per subject, and a salary increase for a whole category of teachers.

whatChanges: A standing fund exists for madaris, covering infrastructure, textbooks, training, scholarships and accreditation.
ALIVE teachers get a training fund and a salary increase.
Textbook assistance is set at a ratio of 1 book per student per subject.
Children of madrasah teachers become eligible for scholarships.
The cost of madaris registration and accreditation is funded.
₱10 million is charged against the Bureau of Madaris’ current appropriations.
readings.insight:
Read this next to Bills 167 and 168 and the picture changes. Three separate bills in this Parliament propose to fund madrasah education: this one from MPs Matalam, Ismael and Alih, Bill 167 from MPs Ampatuan and Mitmug, and Bill 168 from MP Antao. All three were filed within four months of each other in 2023. Bill 167 and this bill overlap substantially — both fund student assistance, teacher support, classroom facilities and textbooks — and their forms of assistance are close enough to read as variations on one draft. Whether they are consolidated is a decision for the committee, and Parliament’s index shows all three sitting in the Committee on Basic, Higher and Technical Education or with Finance alongside it.

The ₱10 million is the number to weigh. It is charged not as new money but against the Bureau of Madaris’ existing appropriations, and it is asked to cover 10 categories including madrasah infrastructure development region-wide and a salary increase for ALIVE teachers. Either the figure is a token first tranche or the list is aspirational; the bill does not say which.

The most concrete thing in it is the textbook ratio. One book per student per subject sounds unremarkable until you have been in a classroom where a book is shared between four children, which in this region is not a rare sight.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates the Bangsamoro Convention Center as a government-owned and controlled corporation with its own legal personality, and puts it in the Municipality of Parang, Maguindanao del Norte.

The Center is to host local and international conventions, meetings, fairs and social events, and to provide the facilities for them — the text names meeting rooms, exhibition halls, auditoriums and accommodation. It may set and collect its own fees and charges, enter contracts, market itself, and form partnerships with private and public entities.

It is run by a board of trustees chaired by the Chief Minister, sitting with the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism, the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Chairman of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Governor of Maguindanao del Norte, and two private sector representatives appointed by the Chief Minister. The board sets policy and appoints a chief executive officer for day-to-day operations, and must issue implementing rules within 60 days. The Center reports annually to the Bangsamoro Government and the relevant committees of Parliament, and is subject to audit.
readings.whyProposed: The declaration of policy is the whole argument: to provide a venue for local and international conventions, meetings, fairs and social events in order to promote economic growth and cultural exchange, and to establish the Bangsamoro as a leading destination for events and gatherings. The region currently has no purpose-built facility at that scale, and hosts its larger gatherings in hotel function rooms, university halls and government buildings.
whoIsAffected: The Municipality of Parang and Maguindanao del Norte, which would host the facility and whose Governor sits on its board.
The regional events, tourism and hospitality trade, which gains a venue and a competitor at the same time.
The Bangsamoro Government, which would carry the cost of building and standing up a corporation.
Organizers of regional gatherings, who currently work around the absence of a large purpose-built venue.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Convention Center, as a government-owned and controlled corporation under the management and supervision of the Bangsamoro Government

A board of trustees chaired by the Chief Minister, with the Ministers of Trade, Investments and Tourism and of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Chairman of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Governor of Maguindanao del Norte, and two private sector appointees
A chief executive officer appointed by the board

funding.detail: No figure appears anywhere in the bill. The amount necessary for initial implementation is to be included in the annual general appropriations act, and the Center is expected to generate funds of its own through fees, charges and partnerships. For a measure whose entire purpose is to build a building, the absence of any construction estimate is the most conspicuous thing in the text.

whatChanges: A Bangsamoro Convention Center exists as a corporation with its own legal personality.
It is sited at Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, rather than at the seat of government.
It can set and keep its own fees and charges and enter its own contracts and partnerships.
The Chief Minister chairs its board and appoints two private sector trustees.
It reports annually to Parliament’s relevant committees and is subject to audit.
readings.insight:
The siting is the decision worth arguing about, and the bill does not argue it. Parang is not the seat of government — Cotabato City is, half an hour away — but Parang holds Polloc port and the region’s freeport, and putting a convention center next to a deepwater harbour rather than next to the ministries is a bet on trade traffic over government traffic. The text states the location in a single clause and gives no reasoning for it.

The second thing is the board. Four of its seven seats are held ex officio by the Chief Minister and ministers, one by a provincial governor, and two by private sector appointees the Chief Minister chooses. A corporation meant to compete for international events is governed almost entirely by people whose day job is something else, and the trade it serves has no seat that is not in the Chief Minister’s gift.

Third, and most practically: the bill authorises a corporation to build and run a convention center and never says what that costs. Every other creation measure of this size in the registry carries at least an initial figure. This one leaves the whole question to the annual appropriations act, which means the decision that matters — how big, and how much — is made after the law rather than in it.

It has moved further than most. The index has it at Second Reading, deferred in July and again in August 2025, which puts it among the handful of bills in this batch past the committee stage.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 144, copy as filed
Parliament Bill No. 151, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires a special help desk for senior citizens and persons with disabilities in every government office and every local government unit in the region.

The desk is where a senior citizen or a person with a disability may make inquiries, ask for assistance and lodge complaints, and it must attend to and address what is brought to it. The bill defines both groups by reference to national law — Republic Act 9994 for senior citizens, any resident citizen at least 60 years old, and Republic Act 10754 for persons with disabilities, using the long-term impairment and barriers formulation.

Section 5 puts the duty on local chief executives by name. Provincial governors, city and municipal mayors must fill the gap in protecting and overseeing the welfare of senior citizens and persons with disabilities in their areas, and all local governments must advocate their rights and take a proactive stance in disseminating information about the benefits and privileges they are entitled to.

The implementing rules are for MSSD to prepare in consultation with MILG within 60 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section is about dignity and access: valuing the dignity of senior citizens and persons with disabilities, guaranteeing full respect for their human rights, and integrating them into mainstream society through programs that ensure easy access to government services.

The practical problem is that the benefits already exist under national law and the barrier is the counter. A person who cannot find out where to go, or who is sent between offices, does not receive an entitlement they legally hold.
whoIsAffected: Senior citizens and persons with disabilities across the region, who gain a named point of contact in every government office.
Every government office and local government unit in BARMM, each of which must staff a desk.
Provincial governors and city and municipal mayors, on whom Section 5 places the duty by name.
MSSD and MILG, which write the implementing rules.
implementedBy: All government offices and local government units in the Bangsamoro, which host the desks
Provincial governors, city and municipal mayors
Ministry of Social Services and Development, with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for the implementing rules

funding.detail: No figure. Funds for establishing the desks in all government offices and LGUs are to be included in the annual appropriations of the region and submitted to Parliament for approval. A desk in every office in the region is mostly a staffing cost, and the bill does not estimate it or say whether existing personnel are to be redesignated.

whatChanges: Every government office and LGU in the region must run a special help desk for senior citizens and persons with disabilities.
The desk handles inquiries, assistance and complaints.
Local chief executives carry a named duty to oversee the welfare of both groups.
Local governments must proactively publicise the benefits and privileges available.
MSSD and MILG must issue implementing rules within 60 days.
readings.insight:
This is a small bill and it is aimed at the right thing. Senior citizen and PWD benefits in the Philippines are generous on paper and unevenly delivered in practice, and the failure is almost always at the counter rather than in the statute. A named desk with a duty to take complaints is a cheap intervention against exactly that failure.

What it lacks is a consequence. There is no penalty, no reporting requirement, no obligation to record what the desk receives, and no one designated to check that the desks exist. A duty to establish a desk, with nobody counting them, is likely to produce a sign on a wall in the offices that were already helpful and nothing at all in the ones that were not. A single annual report from MSSD on how many desks are operating and what they handled would change the character of the bill entirely.

The drafting also leaves the desks unstaffed in the literal sense: the Act says a desk is established, not who sits at it. In a small municipal office that will mean a person already doing something else, which is workable — but it should be said, because the appropriation is meant to pay for it.

On its progress: filed February 2023, First Reading May 2023, and referred in July 2025 to three committees at once — Social Services, Women Youth Children and PWDs, and Finance.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 153, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Free Lunch Act of 2023 institutionalises a free lunch for students in public schools, served five days a week for the whole school year, beginning when classes open.

Schools in three situations are given priority: those with reported severe malnutrition, those in areas of armed conflict, and those in highly congested areas.

A Bangsamoro Free Lunch Council supervises. It is chaired by the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education with the Minister of Health as co-chair, and seats the Ministers of Social Services and Development, of Agriculture, and of the Interior and Local Government. The Council writes the framework that serves as the blueprint — the integrated package of nutrition services, an information database, and the operational detail. MBHTE has primary responsibility for administering the program, working to nutritional standards the Act requires, and a School Lunch Committee operates at school level with duties set out for its members.

The program reports annually to Parliament.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section runs from the right to health and access to essential goods and social services to the specific problem of malnutrition among students, and frames the program as protection for children who by reason of their family’s economic circumstances do not get the nutrition their development requires.

The objectives put the educational case alongside the health one: a child who has not eaten does not learn, so mitigating malnourishment is presented as support for the learning process rather than as welfare attached to a school.
whoIsAffected: Students in public schools across the region, who would receive one free meal on every school day.
Schools in areas of severe malnutrition, armed conflict and congestion, given explicit priority.
Families, for whom a guaranteed school meal is a real reduction in household food cost.
MBHTE, which administers the program, and the four other ministries on the Council.
Local suppliers and producers, through a program feeding public school students five days a week — the Minister of Agriculture sits on the Council.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Free Lunch Council — MBHTE as chair, Health as co-chair, with Social Services and Development, Agriculture, and the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, with primary responsibility for administration
School Lunch Committees at school level

funding.detail: No figure. Funds are to be included in the annual General Appropriations of the Bangsamoro and submitted to Parliament for approval. This is the most expensive recurring commitment in this group of bills by a wide margin — a hot meal for every public school student in the region, five days a week, every week of the school year — and it is the one where the absence of a costing is hardest to defend.

whatChanges: Public school students receive one free lunch on every school day of the year.
The meal is served 5 days a week for the full duration of the school year.
Schools with severe malnutrition, in armed conflict areas, or in congested areas are prioritized.
A five-minister Council supervises and writes the nutrition framework.
Each school runs a School Lunch Committee.
The program reports to Parliament annually.
readings.insight:
The coverage does not match itself, and a committee needs to fix it before anything else. Section 3 institutionalises the program "in all kindergarten and elementary students enrolled in all public schools". Section 11 says the Act covers all public schools in the region and every eligible student enrolled, then defines public schools as "primary and secondary educational institutions". So one section limits the program to kindergarten and elementary, and the other pulls in secondary. The difference is a very large number of students and a very large amount of money.

That matters because the bill carries no figure at all. A daily hot meal for every public school student in BARMM is among the largest recurring programs the region could adopt, and whether it covers elementary only or elementary and secondary changes the cost by a multiple. Leaving both the scope and the price to be settled later leaves nothing to scrutinise.

The Minister of Agriculture’s seat on the Council is the quiet good idea. A guaranteed daily purchase of food for every public school in the region is agricultural demand as much as it is nutrition policy, and putting agriculture on the supervising body is how a feeding program becomes a market for local producers rather than a procurement contract.

The priority list is well chosen and worth noting for what it names: schools in areas of armed conflict, alongside malnutrition and congestion. Few feeding bills anywhere would need that category.

readings.whatItDoes:
This institutionalises a community dispute-resolution system called PASAD — the People’s Alternative System in Addressing Disputes — and builds an office to run it in every province and municipality of the region.

The purpose section states the aim plainly: that people take genuine steps to resolve disputes before certain court actions are begun, and that parties keep the autonomy to settle their differences by a process they agree on. Parties may agree that a dispute is resolved by PASAD; the Ministry of Public Order and Safety then facilitates the constitution of the PASAD Provider the parties choose, and appoints one itself if the parties cannot agree. Providers must be neutral, preferably accredited by MPOS, at least 30 years old, and unrelated by blood or marriage to either party within the third degree.

The process is bounded by confidentiality, with stated exceptions and a waiver mechanism, and by a right of recusal. Where it succeeds, the parties sign a written settlement agreement, the Provider authenticates it and gives them copies, and they may deposit it with the appropriate office where one of them resides. If it has to be enforced, a party may petition a court and may ask the Ministry for help enforcing it.

Section 19 is the section that makes this a Bangsamoro law rather than a generic mediation statute. The Ministry must ensure the PASAD procedure on conciliation, peacemaking and amicable settlement accords with Islamic law — sulh, the tradition of reconciliation — and must also promote the traditional methods used by non-Moro indigenous peoples.

The structure is a Regional Office for PASAD under MPOS, with a secretariat under an Executive Director and three departments: Finance and Administration; Training, Accreditation and Promotion; and Policy, Compliance and Monitoring. Below it sits a Provincial Office under a Provincial Administrator in every BARMM province including the Special Geographic Area, and a Municipal Coordinating Office in every cluster or municipality.
readings.whyProposed:
The stated purpose is speedy, impartial and inexpensive justice through early dispute resolution, and — in the bill’s own phrase — justpeace and sustainable development in the region.

The unstated context is what makes it serious. Formal courts are distant, slow and expensive for most of this region, and disputes that go unresolved here do not simply persist: they escalate into rido, the clan feuding that is among the largest causes of violence and displacement in the Bangsamoro. Sulh and traditional settlement are how most disputes have always actually been resolved. The bill is an attempt to give that a statutory footing, a trained and accredited cadre, and an office structure reaching down to the municipality.
whoIsAffected: Parties to disputes across the region, who gain a settlement route that is faster and cheaper than a court.
Communities affected by rido, where an unsettled dispute is the first step in a feud.
Non-Moro indigenous peoples, whose traditional dispute processes the Ministry is required to promote.
PASAD Providers, a new accredited role with stated qualifications and a recusal duty.

The Ministry of Public Order and Safety, which would carry a regional office, a provincial office in every province and the Special Geographic Area, and a municipal coordinating office in every municipality or cluster.
The courts, which the system is designed to keep certain disputes out of.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety (MPOS), which accredits and where necessary appoints Providers
Regional Office for PASAD under MPOS, with an Executive Director and three service departments
PASAD Provincial Offices under Provincial Administrators, in every province and in the Special Geographic Area
Municipal Coordinating Offices for PASAD in every municipality or cluster
A Technical Working Group organized by the Chief Minister within 1 month of approval, to draft the implementing rules, with an Oversight Committee

funding.detail: No figure. The amount necessary is to be included in the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act of the year following enactment and thereafter — which means, unusually, the Act carries no first-year money at all and the whole structure waits for the next budget cycle. For a bill that creates a regional office, a provincial office in every province and a coordinating office in every municipality, that is a substantial standing cost with no stated size and a one-year delay built into the text.

whatChanges: PASAD becomes a recognized route to settling a dispute, agreed to by the parties.
A settlement reached through it is a written, authenticated agreement that a court can be asked to enforce.
The procedure must be aligned with Islamic law on conciliation and peacemaking, and traditional non-Moro indigenous methods must be promoted.
Providers become an accredited role with stated qualifications, a recusal right and a confidentiality duty.
MPOS gains a PASAD office structure reaching from the region to the municipality.
The Office may recommend statutory changes on dispute resolution directly to Parliament.
readings.insight:
The most consequential thing in this bill is Section 19, and it is one paragraph long. It requires that the whole procedure accord with Islamic law on conciliation and peacemaking, and separately that traditional methods among non-Moro indigenous peoples be promoted. That is the difference between a mediation statute and a Bangsamoro one — it takes sulh, which is how disputes here have in practice always been settled, and gives it a place inside the formal system rather than beside it.

What the bill does not do is make PASAD compulsory. The purpose section says people should take genuine steps to resolve disputes "before certain court actions are instituted", but the operative provision begins with the parties agreeing. No category of dispute is required to go through PASAD first, and no court is directed to send anything to it. Compared with the barangay justice system under national law, which does bar certain suits until conciliation has been attempted, this is an invitation rather than a gate — and the gap between the aspiration in Section 2 and the mechanism in Section 8 is where the bill will be tested.

The funding clause is the practical worry. An office in every province and every municipality is a real payroll, and the Act deliberately takes no money in its first year, deferring everything to the following budget. A dispute-resolution system that exists in law and not yet in the municipalities is worse than none, because parties will have been told to use something that has no one to staff it.

On its progress: filed March 2023, First Reading May 2023, and referred to the Committees on the Bangsamoro Justice System and on Finance in October 2024, where the index leaves it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 159, copy as filed
Parliament Bill No. 160, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This proposes to integrate zakat — the obligatory almsgiving of Islam — with the individual income tax paid by Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government.

The mechanism is set out plainly. An employee’s income tax is reduced by an amount equal to the zakat they pay. The finance officer of the office deducts both, remits the income tax to the Bureau of Internal Revenue, and remits the zakat to the Office of the Lujnatul Uliya of the place, or to its authorised collector. Zakat is computed at 2.5% of net — not gross — income, following the majority Sunni position, which the bill states.

Coverage is confined to government service under BARMM: regular and semi-regular employees, permanent or contractual, and holders of political and appointive positions.

The bill knows it has a problem, and says so. Section 9 requires a representative of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government to sit together and settle the issues. Section 10 then provides that, pending that settlement and national approval, ₱25,000,000 shall be appropriated annually as a subsidy to cover the income tax not remitted to the BIR — the region paying the Bureau the difference, so that no national revenue is lost while the question is unresolved.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section frames it as moral governance: merging what it treats as two obligations of the same character — both, in the bill’s reasoning, levies for public use and public purpose — into a single obligation, so a Muslim employee is not paying twice. The justification section calls the present arrangement a duplicity of obligation and argues that removing it is consistent with the Philippine law of taxation being progressive, regressive and uniform.

Underneath is a real situation. Observant Muslim employees in the region pay income tax to the state and zakat to their community, and for many the combined burden is the reason zakat goes unpaid or is paid without record.
whoIsAffected: Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government — regular, semi-regular, permanent, contractual, political and appointive.
The Office of the Lujnatul Uliya and its authorised zakat collectors, who would receive remitted zakat through a government payroll.
Finance officers in every Bangsamoro government office, who would deduct and remit both.
The Bureau of Internal Revenue, whose collection from these employees would be made whole by a regional subsidy rather than by the taxpayer.
Non-Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government, who are outside the scheme.
The national government, whose agreement Section 9 requires.
implementedBy: Finance officers of Bangsamoro government offices, who deduct and remit
Office of the Lujnatul Uliya, and its authorised collectors of zakat
Bureau of Internal Revenue, which continues to receive the tax — via the subsidy, pending settlement
A joint discussion of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government, required by Section 9

funding.detail: ₱25,000,000 annually, appropriated as a subsidy to pay the Bureau of Internal Revenue the income tax that employees do not remit because they have paid zakat instead. The subsidy is expressly a holding arrangement — it runs "pending settlement of the issues and approval thereof by the National Government". It is one of the few precise figures in this batch and it buys time rather than a service.

whatChanges: A Muslim employee’s income tax is reduced by the zakat they pay, at 2.5% of net income.
Zakat is deducted at payroll and remitted to the Lujnatul Uliya by the employing office.
The Bangsamoro Government appropriates ₱25 million a year to make the BIR whole in the meantime.
The Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government are required to meet and settle the legal question.
readings.insight:
This is the most legally exposed bill in this batch, and the striking thing is that its drafters clearly knew it.

Individual income tax is a national tax, imposed by the National Internal Revenue Code and collected by the BIR. A regional parliament cannot reduce a national tax liability, and the Bangsamoro Organic Law does not give the region that power. The bill does not pretend otherwise. Section 9 requires the region, the Darul Ifta and the national government to sit down over it, and Section 10 provides ₱25 million a year so that until they do, the national treasury loses nothing and the employee’s zakat still reaches the Lujnatul Uliya. That is an unusually honest structure: it converts a jurisdictional claim the region cannot yet make into a subsidy the region can pay, and it leaves the constitutional question open on the face of the statute.

The second question is one the bill does not address. The scheme routes a payroll deduction from a government office to a religious body, and confers a fiscal benefit that depends on the employee’s religion. Those raise establishment and equal protection questions under the Constitution that Section 9’s discussion would have to reach.

A drafting point that matters practically: the bill repeatedly says "individual income tax return" where it means the tax itself. A return is a form. The distinction would need fixing before enactment, because the operative sections deduct and remit something that, as written, is a document.

On its progress: filed February 2023, First Reading May 2023, deferred in July 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
This gives Bangsamoro voters the power to make regional law themselves, and sets out every step of how.

The power covers propositions to enact, amend or repeal regional legislation, and is exercised by registered voters of the region. Five things are off limits, among them propositions embracing more than one subject and propositions outside the powers of the Bangsamoro Government or inside the reserved powers of the national government.

The procedure runs like this. Proponents first send the proposed text to the Bangsamoro Attorney General and ask for a circulating title and summary and a unique numerical identifier. Once issued, they have 180 days to gather signatures. The petition is filed with the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which certifies whether it is sufficient and whether the signatures are authentic. An Initiatives Coordinator is provided for.

The threshold is the heart of it: a proposition qualifies as a ballot measure if signed by at least 10% of all registered voters of the region, reckoned from the immediately preceding election, and — for propositions affecting the whole region — every parliamentary district must be represented by at least 3%. A plebiscite follows.

The bill then does something a plain initiative statute would not. Section 18 limits Parliament: a proposition approved by initiative cannot be repealed, modified or amended within 6 months, may only be repealed by Parliament within 3 years, and any law seeking to repeal a law enacted by initiative is itself subject to a referendum. Section 19 provides a separate, gentler route — a people-initiated bill, filed by petition with Parliament for it to consider in the ordinary way.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Organic Law contemplates a system of initiative and referendum for the region, and until it is legislated the power exists on paper and cannot be exercised. This bill supplies the machinery: who may propose, what may be proposed, how a petition is titled and circulated, how many signatures are needed and from where, who certifies them, and what happens after a proposition passes.
whoIsAffected: Every registered voter in the Bangsamoro, who gains a route to legislate directly.
The Bangsamoro Parliament, whose power to amend or repeal a successful initiative is expressly restricted for 3 years.
The Bangsamoro Attorney General, given the gatekeeping function of issuing the circulating title and summary.
The Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which must verify signatures at region-wide scale and run the plebiscites.
Civil society and advocacy groups, for whom this is the mechanism to put a measure Parliament will not take up to a vote.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which certifies sufficiency and authenticity and conducts the plebiscite
Office of the Bangsamoro Attorney General, which issues the circulating title, the summary and the numerical identifier
An Initiatives Coordinator provided for in the Act
The Bangsamoro Parliament, for the people-initiated bill route and for the adoption provision

funding.detail: No figure. Initial implementation is charged against the current year’s appropriations of the agencies named in the Act, and later years go into the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act. Verifying signatures from 10% of the region’s registered voters and running a region-wide plebiscite are both expensive, and the cost falls first on the Bangsamoro Electoral Office out of a budget already set.

whatChanges: Registered voters can propose regional legislation directly and put it to a plebiscite.
A proposition needs 10% of the region’s registered voters, with at least 3% from every parliamentary district for region-wide measures.
Proponents get 180 days to gather signatures after the Attorney General issues the circulating title.
Parliament cannot touch a successful initiative for 6 months and can only repeal it within 3 years — and a repealing law must itself go to a referendum.
A separate route lets voters file a bill with Parliament by petition.
Propositions embracing more than one subject, or outside Bangsamoro competence, are barred.
readings.insight:
The district floor is the design decision that will decide whether this power is ever used. Requiring 10% of all registered voters region-wide is a high bar on its own; requiring in addition that every parliamentary district supply at least 3% means an initiative cannot be carried by a concentrated majority in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao alone. It has to reach into the island districts and into every constituency. That is a deliberate protection for the smaller and more distant parts of the region against a mainland majority, and it is also, in a region with this geography and these transport costs, a very hard signature drive to run.

Section 18 is the more unusual provision and it is genuinely strong. Most initiative statutes let the legislature amend what the people pass; this one bars Parliament from touching it for 6 months, restricts repeal to a 3-year window, and then requires any repealing law to go to a referendum of its own. That makes a successful initiative harder to undo than an ordinary act of Parliament, which is a real transfer of power away from the chamber that would be passing this bill.

Worth noting what it does not cover. Section 4 confines the power to regional legislation and leaves initiatives on all other legislative acts to existing law, so this is not a route to amending the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which is national legislation.

On its progress: filed March 2023, First Reading June 2023, deferred in August 2024 and referred to the Committee on Rules that same month, where it sits.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 165, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Madaris Education Assistance Act of 2023 puts money into private Islamic schools — madaris — by paying three different recipients directly.

Students get tuition of not less than ₱1,000 a year, reading materials, and a nutrition and feeding program for the young ones. Teachers — gurus, the bill uses the Arabic term and defines it — get an allowance of not less than ₱2,000 a month plus a faculty education development program. The madrasah itself gets classroom facilities, named down to desks, tables and chalkboards, and textbook assistance.

The faculty program is the most substantial piece: scholarships for master’s and doctorate degrees, in the country and outside it, plus seminars and training. Anyone who qualifies to study abroad must sign an undertaking to return and serve for a period set against the length of the scholarship.

Eligibility is narrow and stated. Priority goes to students whose family income is not more than ₱40,000 a year. Assistance runs only to Muslim students who are Filipino citizens and residents of the Bangsamoro, who are not already receiving another government scholarship, who are enrolled in a madrasah, and who have not transferred to one outside the region. MBHTE, through the Bureau of Madaris Education, sets the criteria, accredits which madaris qualify, and assesses whether the schools receiving the money are still teaching well.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section grounds it in Section 16, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law — the mandate to establish and maintain a complete and adequate system of education responsive to the needs and aspirations of the Bangsamoro people — and says the way to improve quality in the madaris is to assist the teachers and the students directly.

The unstated premise is that madaris are community-based and privately operated. They sit outside the public school funding system, they teach a large share of Bangsamoro children, and until something like this passes there is no standing mechanism for regional money to reach them.
whoIsAffected: Students in madaris across the region, with priority to those whose family income is ₱40,000 a year or less.
Gurus, who would receive a monthly allowance and access to postgraduate scholarships abroad.
Madaris as institutions, which would receive classroom furniture and textbooks.
Students already holding another government scholarship, who are expressly excluded.
Non-Muslim students, who are outside the stated coverage.
MBHTE and the Bureau of Madaris Education, which would have to build an accreditation system to run any of it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education (MBHTE), for policy guidance, monitoring and the implementing rules
Bureau of Madaris Education (BME), which delivers the assistance and, with MBHTE, sets the income criterion

funding.detail: No total is stated. MBHTE determines the amount necessary for initial implementation, and later years go into the annual Bangsamoro appropriations. The only hard figures in the bill are the floors on individual benefits — not less than ₱1,000 per student per year and not less than ₱2,000 per guru per month — and the ₱40,000 annual family income mark that sets priority.

whatChanges: Regional money reaches privately operated madaris for the first time through a standing mechanism.
Gurus gain a monthly allowance with a floor of ₱2,000 and access to postgraduate scholarships.
Students in madaris gain a tuition subsidy, reading materials and a feeding program.
MBHTE must build an accreditation policy to determine which madaris qualify.
Assistance is conditioned on continued quality, which MBHTE is required to assess.
readings.insight:
Every benefit in this bill is a floor rather than a figure. Not less than ₱1,000 a year, not less than ₱2,000 a month: generous drafting in one sense, because nothing caps what MBHTE may pay, and empty in another, because the bill sets no total and MBHTE decides the initial appropriation itself. What the law guarantees is a minimum per head; what it costs is settled somewhere else entirely.

The floors themselves are worth reading against the region. ₱1,000 a year in tuition and ₱2,000 a month for a teacher are modest sums, and the ₱40,000 annual family income that triggers priority is well under the national poverty threshold for a family of five — which means the priority mark will catch a very large share of the households the bill is aimed at rather than distinguishing between them.

The scholarship clause is the quiet ambition in it. Master’s and doctorate study abroad for madrasah teachers, with a return-service undertaking, is a serious investment in a teaching corps that has largely had no route to formal postgraduate credentials.

The coverage clause runs to Muslim students only. In a region with substantial non-Muslim indigenous communities that is a real limit, though it follows from what a madrasah is; it is stated here because the bill states it and a reader should not have to infer it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 167, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
Where Bill 167 pays for madrasah education as it exists, this one proposes to rebuild the curriculum underneath it.

The bill creates a Special Madrasah Fund to review, redesign, pilot test and then implement a balanced basic madrasah curriculum from Grade 1 to Senior High School. "Balanced" is the operative word and the text defines it at length: curricula that are interactively balanced for the spiritual and worldly development of the learner, that integrate the core subjects of mainstream basic education in deeply contextualised form, and that guarantee parallelism with — the text says if not superiority to — what DepEd prescribes for standard madaris.

The method is set out as a sequence. Existing curricula and textbooks are reviewed and redesigned; a Project Management Team merges related subjects to cut what the bill calls information overload; the result is field-tested in at least two qualified madaris for elementary and two for secondary in each province and in the Special Geographic Area; it is enhanced on the results, adopted in transition elsewhere for terminal validation, packaged, and then implemented by at least one madrasah for each level in every municipality and city in the region.

Governance sits with a Special Madrasah Fund Board chaired by the Directorate General for Madaris Education, with the Directorate Generals for Basic and Technical Education as associate chairpersons, and members drawn from the most prominent regional madaris association, the dominant registered ulama federation, and the regional offices of DepEd, TESDA, the Commission on Muslim Filipinos and the finance ministry. The Chief Minister appoints them for three years and may revoke an appointment for disgraceful or immoral conduct or corrupt practice. Board membership must be balanced across expertise in Islamic scholarship, curriculum development, school management, and fund administration.

The destination is accreditation. The bill’s stated ultimate goal is that DepEd recognize the madrasah as a Standard Muslim Education Institution and issue Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificates, so a madrasah completer can transfer into the state system, enrol at the next level, or present the certificate as an educational qualification for a job.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note makes an argument few filed bills bother with. It says the balanced madrasah is idealised and does not exist: the madaris DepEd accredits as Standard Private Madrasah are balanced only in the sense that five core subjects have been added on top of the Qur’an, Seerah, Hadith, Aqeedah, Fiqh and Arabic, which produces information overload rather than integration. It cites the Constitution’s education article and Section 16 of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, and it argues its theological case from Surah Al-Qasas 28:77 and a hadith on not surrendering either world for the other.

The practical driver is the Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificate. Without it, years spent in a madrasah convert into nothing a state school or an employer will count.
whoIsAffected: Madrasah learners from Grade 1 to Senior High School, whose curriculum and textbooks would be rewritten.
Madrasah completers, for whom the accreditation certificate would convert years of study into a recognized qualification.
The madaris selected for pilot testing — at least 2 for elementary and 2 for secondary in each province and in the Special Geographic Area — and eventually at least one per municipality or city.
Gurus, who would teach a merged and rewritten subject set.
DepEd and TESDA, whose recognition the whole design depends on and who sit on the board.
The regional madaris association and the ulama federation, given seats on the board that governs the fund.
implementedBy: Special Madrasah Fund Board, chaired by the Directorate General for Madaris Education with the Directorate Generals for Basic Education and Technical Education as associate chairpersons, appointed by the Chief Minister for 3 years
A Project Management Team, recruited by the Board and approved by the MBHTE Minister, which prepares a 10-year development and operational plan and runs the review, rewriting and pilot testing
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Department of Education, whose accreditation and equivalency certificate is the stated end point, in collaboration with MBHTE

funding.detail: No total is stated. Initial implementation is charged against the current year’s Bangsamoro appropriations and later years go into the annual General Appropriations Act. The bill does itemise what the money is for, which is more than most: curriculum and textbook review and development, reproduction of new textbooks, pilot testing in each province and the Special Geographic Area, and construction of pilot testing building units, specified as a 7-room unit of one office and six classrooms.

whatChanges: A standing fund exists to redesign the basic madrasah curriculum from Grade 1 to Senior High School.
Subjects are merged to reduce overload, and mainstream core subjects are integrated in contextualised form.
A board seating madaris and ulama organizations alongside DepEd, TESDA and the finance ministry governs the fund.
A 10-year development and operational plan is required, with budget allocations attached.
Curricula are pilot tested province by province before general adoption, then rolled out to at least one madrasah per level per municipality or city.
Buildings are funded for the pilot sites, at a specified 7-room configuration.
readings.insight:
The whole design turns on something the Bangsamoro Parliament cannot legislate. The Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificate is issued by DepEd, a national department, and the bill can fund the curriculum, staff the board and run the pilots but cannot make DepEd recognize the result. The text is careful about this — it says the measure creates the "potentiality" that DepEd would accredit, and that the mechanics are for the Department to set in collaboration with MBHTE. That is honest drafting, and it also means the bill’s stated ultimate goal is an outcome it can only make more likely.

The appropriations clause has aged. It names the provinces where pilot testing is to happen and the list includes Sulu, which the Supreme Court removed from the Bangsamoro in 2024, after this bill was filed in May 2023. Section 5, which sets out the same pilot design, refers instead to "every province of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region" and the Special Geographic Area — wording that survives the change. The two clauses now describe different maps.

One more thing worth noticing: the board seats are drawn from the "most prominent" regional madaris association and the "most dominant" registered ulama federation. Neither superlative is defined, and in a region with several competing ulama bodies, deciding which one is dominant is a political act the bill hands to whoever makes the appointment.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 168, copy as filed
Parliament Bill No. 174, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates, in every barangay of every city and municipality, a Barangay Justice System Multi-Sectoral Traditional and Customary Laws Advisory Council — a body to advise the barangay justice system on the customary law of the community it is settling disputes in.

The Council is chaired by the city or municipal mayor and seats a representative of the city or municipal police office, a purok leader, a traditional leader, a religious leader, an indigenous people’s leader, a tribal leader, and representatives of women, youth and persons with disabilities, each drawn from the barangay concerned.

Its functions are advisory and expressly without prejudice to the Katarungang Pambarangay Law, the national barangay justice statute. It provides specialised information, skills and experience on the community’s existing traditional and customary laws to aid the people running the barangay justice system; provides guidance and technical advice in areas outside the Lupon members’ usual expertise; encourages retirees from government and the private sector to join the barangay justice system; supplies customary and traditional laws that have fallen out of use through non-practice; and acts as the system’s advocate in the barangay.

Mayors must convene the Councils within 6 months of approval. Members receive no remuneration.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section is short and states the aim: that the customs, beliefs and traditions of the Bangsamoro people are recognized, respected and guaranteed, and that disputes are resolved justly and peacefully.

The practical case is that the Lupong Tagapamayapa — the barangay conciliation panel under national law — applies a national framework in communities whose disputes are actually governed by customary law, whether Moro or indigenous. The Council is meant to put that knowledge at the panel’s disposal rather than leave it to whichever member happens to have it.
whoIsAffected: Parties to barangay-level disputes, whose settlement would draw on customary law explicitly.
Lupong Tagapamayapa members, who gain an advisory body for matters outside their expertise.
Traditional, religious, indigenous and tribal leaders, given a formal role in the barangay justice system.
Women, youth and persons with disabilities, each given a seat.
City and municipal mayors, who chair every one of these Councils in their jurisdiction and must convene them within 6 months.
implementedBy: City and municipal mayors, as chairs and as the officials required to convene the Councils
The Councils themselves, in every barangay
City and municipal police offices, which supply a representative to each

funding.detail: The bill makes no appropriation and states that members receive no remuneration for their duties. It is designed to cost nothing, which is a defensible choice for an advisory body — and also the reason to ask how often bodies with no budget and no paid members actually meet.

whatChanges: Every barangay in the region gains a customary law advisory council for its justice system.
Traditional, religious, indigenous and tribal leaders acquire a formal advisory role.
Women, youth and PWD representatives sit on the council by right.
Customary laws that have fallen out of use through non-practice are to be supplied back to the system.
Mayors must convene the councils within 6 months of approval.
The Katarungang Pambarangay Law is expressly unaffected.
readings.insight:
The chairmanship does not scale, and it is the first thing a committee should look at. The Council exists in every barangay, and the chair of every one of them is the city or municipal mayor. Lanao del Sur has municipalities with dozens of barangays; a mayor there would chair dozens of separate councils. The bill gives no provision for a designated representative, no quorum rule, and no meeting schedule. As drafted, the person who must sit at the head of each council is the one person in the municipality who cannot be in all of them.

The function about disused customary law is the most interesting line in the bill and the least noticed. Providing the barangay justice system with "customary and traditional laws that may not have been in use for reasons of non-practice" is a revival mandate, not merely an advisory one — it invites councils to bring back rules that fell out of use. Whether that is restoration or invention will depend entirely on who sits on the council, which is why the composition matters as much as it does.

The seats for women, youth and persons with disabilities are worth noting for what they do in this context. Customary dispute resolution in the region is, in practice, largely conducted by senior men. Writing those three seats into the statute is a deliberate correction, and it sits in tension with the traditional and tribal leadership seats beside it in a way the bill leaves unresolved.

Read alongside Bill 159, which builds a whole PASAD office structure for alternative dispute resolution, this is the same instinct at a fraction of the cost — and both are before the Committee on the Bangsamoro Justice System.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 176, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires all signage in the Bangsamoro, in both public and private institutions and establishments, to be in English and Arabic.

The two must appear together — written side by side, or English above and Arabic below. Signage is defined broadly: any written announcement installed, posted, hung, painted or otherwise displayed in a public place, and generally any graphic display intended to convey information to an audience. The Ministry of Public Works is to provide a list of all appropriate and lawful signages and other devices and instruments.

Funds come from the Bangsamoro appropriations act. The Act takes effect 15 days after publication in at least two newspapers of regional circulation.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy states it as inclusivity: the Bangsamoro Government respects and promotes inclusivity within the region, and to that end mandates English-Arabic signage in public and private establishments.

Arabic is the liturgical language of Islam and the language of madrasah instruction across the region, and its visible presence in public space is a marker of the Bangsamoro identity the autonomy arrangement exists to express.
whoIsAffected: Every private establishment in the region — shops, restaurants, offices, clinics — which would have to replace or supplement its signage.
Every public institution and government office in the region.
The Ministry of Public Works, which must issue the list of appropriate and lawful signages.
Readers of Arabic, for whom public information becomes accessible.
Speakers of the region’s own languages — Maguindanaon, Maranao, Tausug, Sinama, Yakan, Iranun — and of Filipino, none of which the bill provides for.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW), which provides the list of appropriate and lawful signages, devices and instruments

funding.detail: No figure. Funds are charged against the General Appropriation Act of the Bangsamoro. The appropriation would cover government signage; the bill also binds every private establishment in the region and says nothing about who pays for theirs, which is the larger cost by far and falls on the businesses.

whatChanges: All signage in the region, public and private, must be in English and Arabic.
The two languages must appear together — side by side, or English above Arabic.
MPW must publish a list of appropriate and lawful signages.
Government signage costs come from the Bangsamoro appropriations act.
readings.insight:
Section 4 defines "Official Language" as "English-Arabic, to be used in signages" — and that definition is where the difficulty is. Under the Constitution the national language is Filipino, and the official languages are Filipino and English. The Bangsamoro Organic Law treats Arabic as an official language of the region alongside Filipino and English, so Arabic on public signage is on solid ground; what is not is a signage rule that requires English and Arabic and leaves Filipino out entirely.

The compliance cost is the second thing, and it is not small. The bill binds every private establishment in the region and provides money only through the regional appropriations act, which will not be paying for the signage of shops in Bongao or Marawi. Nor is there a transition period, a threshold exempting small businesses, or a penalty — so the Act takes effect 15 days after publication and every non-compliant sign in the region is immediately non-compliant with no stated consequence, which is a strange combination.

Third, and most substantively: the region has six or more living languages of its own. A signage law justified by inclusivity that mandates Arabic and English while making no provision for Maguindanaon, Maranao, Tausug, Sinama, Yakan or Iranun is making a particular argument about what Bangsamoro identity consists of. That is a legitimate argument to make and the bill should be read as making it.

It carries 9 principal authors, among the most in this batch, which suggests the argument is widely shared.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Integrated Coastal Management Act of 2023 makes integrated coastal management the region’s official policy framework for its coasts and seas, and builds a council to run it.

Section 3 is the substance: integrated coastal management and related approaches, coastal resource management among them, become the regional management policy framework for the sustainable development of the region’s coastal and marine environment — aimed at food security, sustainable livelihood, poverty alleviation and reduced vulnerability to natural hazards, while preserving ecological integrity. The Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy is then to issue guidelines for coastal zoning: delineating coastal areas, identifying land uses, and regulating activity in the coastal zone.

The Integrated Coastal Management Council is chaired by the MENRE Minister and seats the Ministers of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and of Trade, Investments and Tourism, the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, the Directors-General for Environment and Natural Resources and for Fisheries, two representatives of accredited civil society organizations, and representatives from coastal communities in every province.

The Council oversees implementation, develops and implements a Coastal Management Plan, provides measures to protect mangroves, coral reefs and seagrasses, coordinates with law enforcement against destructive fishing and pollution, works with the trade ministry on ecotourism and sustainable fisheries, and works with the interior ministry to bring local governments and coastal communities into the process through consultations, capacity building and awareness work.

Costs are charged against MENRE’s existing budget and thereafter to the annual appropriations act. The Act would take effect 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation in the region.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note is unusually specific for a framework bill. BARMM holds mangroves, seagrass beds and coral reefs that carry ecological, economic and cultural weight; fisheries and aquaculture are the primary income for many communities and depend directly on the health of those systems; and the coast is also the region’s transport network. Against that it sets overfishing, pollution, habitat destruction, and climate change through sea level rise and warming water — and adds that conflict in coastal areas compounds the degradation. The remedy it proposes is regulation of fishing practice, pollution reduction, marine protected areas, and education.
whoIsAffected: Coastal and fishing communities across the region, who would gain named representation on the Council — one or more from every province — and whose fishing practices the framework is meant to regulate.
The island provinces above all, where the coast is not a margin but the entire economy.
Local government units with coastal jurisdiction, brought into the process through MILG.
Accredited civil society organizations, given two seats.
Operators in ecotourism, aquaculture and commercial fishing, whose activities the coastal zoning guidelines would regulate.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy (MENRE), which chairs the Council and issues the coastal zoning guidelines
Integrated Coastal Management Council (ICMC)
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Agrarian Reform, and Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for local government and community participation
Directors-General for Environment and Natural Resources and for Fisheries
Law enforcement agencies, with which the Council is to coordinate rather than direct

funding.detail: No sum is stated and no new money is created. The amount necessary is charged against MENRE’s current budget and thereafter included in the annual appropriations act — which means, in the first year, the Council and the Coastal Management Plan are funded by MENRE finding room for them inside a budget already committed.

whatChanges: Integrated coastal management becomes the region’s stated policy framework rather than a project approach.
MENRE must issue coastal zoning guidelines delineating coastal areas and regulating activity within them.
A standing Council exists with ministers, directors-general, civil society and coastal community representation.
A Coastal Management Plan is required, developed and implemented by the Council.
Mangroves, coral reefs and seagrasses acquire a named body responsible for measures to protect them.
Coastal communities gain seats at the table where their fisheries are regulated.
readings.insight:
This is a coordination bill, and reading it as anything stronger would misread it. The Council oversees, develops, provides measures and coordinates; it does not license, penalise or enforce. There are no penalties anywhere in the text. Enforcement against destructive fishing stays with the law enforcement agencies the Council coordinates with, and the operative regulatory instrument — the coastal zoning guidelines — is MENRE’s to write after the fact. What the bill actually delivers on the day it takes effect is a policy declaration, a council, and an obligation to produce a plan.

The funding clause is the constraint that matters. Charging a new regional framework to a ministry’s current budget, with no additional appropriation in the first year, is how coordination bodies end up meeting rarely and producing plans slowly.

One structural gap is worth flagging because it will be the first thing the Council fights about. The membership includes two civil society representatives and "representatives from coastal communities in every province" — unnumbered — and Section 5 leaves the mechanism for selecting both to the Council’s own first regular meeting. So the size of the Council and the question of who speaks for a coastal community are settled by the Council itself, after it has already been convened by the ministers and directors-general who are on it by office.

The bill is among the furthest advanced in this batch, sitting at Second Reading since October 2025.

Parliament Bill No. 186, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Breastfeeding Facilities Act of 2023 requires every government and private establishment in the region to provide a private area or room for breastfeeding or expressing milk.

The facility must be easily accessible and conveniently located within the premises, and must have comfortable seating, electrical outlets, a table or other flat surface, and a sink for washing hands and equipment.

All employers must give breastfeeding employees lactation breaks of not less than 30 minutes in total for every four-hour work period, in addition to the rest periods the law already provides, and employees may not be penalised or discriminated against for taking them.

Violation of any provision carries a fine of not less than ₱10,000 and not more than ₱50,000 for each violation, applying to government officials and employees as well as to private establishments. The Ministry of Health, with the Ministry of Labor and Employment, issues the implementing rules within 60 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section states it directly: to protect, promote and support breastfeeding as the normal and optimal way of feeding infants, and to that end to establish facilities in government and private establishments so mothers can breastfeed or express milk comfortably and safely.

The practical barrier the bill addresses is that a mother returning to work without a private space and a protected break stops breastfeeding, whatever the health guidance says.
whoIsAffected: Breastfeeding mothers in employment across the region.
Every government and private establishment in the Bangsamoro, which must build or designate a facility.
All employers, who must grant lactation breaks of at least 30 minutes per four-hour work period.
Government officials and employees, who are personally liable to the fine.
Infants, as the beneficiaries the health case rests on.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, in coordination with the Ministry of Labor and Employment, for the implementing rules
Government and private establishments, which provide the facilities and the breaks

funding.detail: The bill makes no appropriation. The cost falls on establishments — a room with seating, a power outlet, a surface and a sink — and the Act is enforced by fine rather than funded by subsidy. Government offices would carry their own compliance cost out of existing budgets.

whatChanges: Every government and private establishment in the region must provide a breastfeeding facility.
The facility has a specified minimum fit-out: seating, electrical outlets, a flat surface and a sink.
Employers must grant at least 30 minutes of lactation break per four-hour work period, on top of normal rest periods.
Penalising or discriminating against an employee for taking the break is prohibited.
Violations carry a fine of ₱10,000 to ₱50,000 each.
readings.insight:
This is one of only two bills in this batch of 25 that carries a penalty, and that alone makes it worth attention. Most measures here create a council, declare a policy or promise an appropriation; this one states a duty, specifies the fit-out in enough detail that compliance can be checked by looking, and attaches ₱10,000 to ₱50,000 to each failure. It is the most enforceable thing in the group.

The fine reaches government officials and employees personally, not just their offices — which is unusual, and is the provision most likely to be softened in committee.

What the drafting does not do is scale the duty. "All government and private establishments" means the same obligation applies to a regional ministry and to a two-person sari-sari store, with no floor by employee count or floor area and no transition period. National law on the same subject works through a graduated scheme with exemptions for establishments where compliance is not practicable; this bill has none, which will make the implementing rules carry more weight than they should.

The break formula is worth stating plainly because it is generous and easy to misread: not less than 30 minutes in total for every four-hour work period, which on a standard eight-hour day is an hour, on top of existing rest periods.

On its progress: filed May 2023, First Reading June 2023, referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children and Persons with Disability in February 2025.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 196, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This declares the regional holidays of the Bangsamoro and sets up the machinery for local ones.

Five are declared as regional non-working holidays in addition to the national holidays: Bangsamoro Foundation Day on 21 January; Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, both on movable dates; Jabidah Commemoration Day on 18 March; and Sheik Karimul Makhdum Day on 7 November.

Because the two Eids move, the Act provides that their dates are determined by the Hijri calendar, by sighting of the moon, or by Islamic astronomical calculation, whichever is possible or convenient — and that the Chief Minister, coordinating with the Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta, proclaims the date at least 3 days beforehand.

Local special holidays are handled separately. The Chief Minister may by proclamation allow observance of LGU anniversaries and other events of religious or historical significance, provided the unit notifies and seeks sanction at least 15 days ahead. Within 90 days the leagues of provinces, cities and municipalities must each submit a master list of existing local holidays — nature, legal basis and date of declaration — which is then furnished to the Office of the Chief Minister. A holiday economics provision asks that local special holidays fall on a Monday where possible, with the local sanggunian able to move one to the nearest Monday if it declares the change at least 3 months ahead.

The holidays are observed by all private and public offices and corporations, with the Labor Code applying to private sector employees, and a pretermission rule handles acts due on a holiday.
readings.whyProposed:
Section 4 grounds the declaration in Republic Act 11054, the Bangsamoro Organic Law, and in Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, which mandates Parliament to enact a law identifying the holidays to be observed in the region.

So this is a bill Parliament was directed to pass. What is discretionary is which days it chose.
whoIsAffected: Everyone working in the region, public and private, for whom five days become non-working.
Private sector employees specifically, whose holiday pay is governed by the Labor Code under Section 10.
Local government units, which must route their anniversary observances through the Chief Minister with 15 days’ notice.
The leagues of provinces, cities and municipalities, which must compile master lists within 90 days.
The Bangsamoro Darul Ifta, whose Mufti is consulted on the movable dates.
Anyone with a legal deadline falling on one of these days, covered by the pretermission rule.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, which proclaims the Eid dates and sanctions local special holidays
The Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta, coordinating on the movable dates
The leagues of provinces, cities and municipalities, which submit the master lists
Local sanggunians, which may move a local holiday to the nearest Monday

funding.detail: No appropriation and none needed for the declaration itself. The real cost of a non-working holiday is borne by employers through holiday pay under the Labor Code and by the government through lost working days, and the bill does not attempt to estimate either.

whatChanges: Five regional non-working holidays are declared on top of the national ones.
The Eid dates are proclaimed by the Chief Minister with the Darul Ifta, at least 3 days ahead.
Local anniversaries become special non-working holidays on the Chief Minister’s proclamation, with 15 days’ notice.
A master list of all existing local special holidays is compiled within 90 days.
Local special holidays are to fall on a Monday where possible.
Acts due on a holiday roll over under the pretermission rule.
readings.insight:
The choice of days is the substance, and it is a deliberate statement about what the Bangsamoro remembers.

Jabidah Commemoration Day, 18 March, marks the 1968 Jabidah massacre on Corregidor — the killing of Moro recruits that is generally treated as the beginning of the modern Moro struggle and, through it, of everything that led to this region existing. Sheik Karimul Makhdum Day, 7 November, honors the missionary who reached Simunul in Tawi-Tawi in 1380 and built the first mosque in the Philippines. One day marks the grievance the autonomy came from; the other marks the faith it is built on. Placing them beside the two Eids and a foundation day is the bill’s actual argument, and it makes it without a word of explanation.

The 3-day notice for the Eids is the practical provision most likely to cause friction, and it is a genuine constraint rather than an oversight: the date genuinely cannot be fixed further out where moon sighting governs. But 3 days is very short for schools, airlines, hospitals and payroll, and the Act’s own alternative — Islamic astronomical calculation, which can be done a year ahead — sits in the same sentence. Which method prevails is left as "whichever is possible or convenient", and that phrase will do a lot of work.

The filed copy has two Section 5s: one headed DATE OF OBSERVANCE and the next LOCAL SPECIAL HOLIDAYS. Everything after is numbered from the second, so the Act as drafted has no Section 5 uniquely identifying either. Anyone citing a section of this measure should quote the heading as well as the number.

Section 6 refers a duty to "the BCPCH" without expanding the acronym anywhere in the filed text.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 219, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Regional Infrastructure Geo-tagging Act of 2023 requires every infrastructure project the Bangsamoro Government builds to be geo-tagged at every stage and published on a public portal.

Geo-tagging is defined as attaching location metadata — latitude and longitude — to the physical site of a project and uploading it, together with the project name, the location and the cost, so that government, citizens and other stakeholders can check progress in real time. The projects covered are listed and the list is broad: roads, bridges, ports, flood control, water supply, schools, multipurpose buildings, government buildings, hospitals and health facilities, barangay and municipal halls, centers, housing, and other horizontal and vertical works.

On effectivity, all such projects must be geo-tagged at every stage using a GPS-enabled phone or other GPS and image-capture device, and uploaded to a regional online portal the Act creates. Every implementing agency must also carry a portal on its own official website where information for a specific project location can be found, feeding the regional one.

Around that sit implementing guidelines, an information and education campaign, rules on access and the regional portal, a requirement for regular data updates with cybersecurity measures, and capacity building.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section runs from the constitutional policy of full public disclosure and the role of information in nation-building to the Bangsamoro Government’s own principle of Moral Governance — and states the aim in unusually blunt terms: improving accountability for the physical and financial outcomes of government infrastructure projects, eliminating corruption, and ensuring multi-stakeholder participation.

The method is the national geo-tagging practice used in agriculture and public works, applied region-wide and made statutory rather than administrative.
whoIsAffected: Every implementing agency of the Bangsamoro Government that builds anything.
Contractors, whose work becomes photographically and geographically documented at each stage.
Citizens and civil society, who gain project name, location and cost on a public portal.
The Ministry of Public Works and the Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology Office, which build the portal and run capacity building.
Communities in remote areas, where a project’s existence is hardest to verify from the capital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW) and the Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology office (BICT), which establish the Regional Infrastructure Portal
All implementing agencies, which geo-tag their projects and host agency portals

funding.detail: ₱20,000,000 initial appropriation, made available to MPW, BICT and the other ministries to establish the online Regional Infrastructure Portal and to assist and train agencies in setting up portals on their own websites. Thereafter each implementing agency carries the cost in its regular budget. It is one of the few precise appropriations in this batch and it is a modest one for a region-wide system.

whatChanges: Every Bangsamoro infrastructure project must be geo-tagged at every stage of implementation.
Project name, location and cost go on a public portal, updated as work proceeds.
Each implementing agency must host its own project portal, feeding the regional one.
Data updates are periodic and subject to cybersecurity measures.
Agencies receive capacity building to do it.
₱20 million is appropriated to build the system.
readings.insight:
This is the most straightforwardly useful bill in the batch and one of the cheapest. Publishing a photograph, a coordinate and a cost for every project at every stage is the single most effective check there is against the project that is paid for and never built, or built at a fraction of the specification. It requires no new agency, no commission and no council — three things almost every other bill here creates.

It carries 17 principal authors, far more than anything else in this group, which is a fair indication of how uncontroversial the proposition is.

The question a committee should press is what happens when an agency does not comply. There is no penalty, no consequence for a project that appears on no portal, and no provision making disbursement conditional on the geo-tag being uploaded. The obvious fix is the one used elsewhere: tie the release of a progress payment to the upload. Without something of that kind, the register will be complete for the agencies that were already transparent.

The ₱20 million is for the portal, the training and the assistance; thereafter each agency funds its own compliance from its regular budget. That is the right structure, and it also means the recurring cost is invisible in this bill.

On its progress: filed June 2023, First Reading July 2023, and referred to the Committees on Public Works and on Finance in May 2025.
